name: The Approved Tool List
title: The Approved Tool List
answer: The approved tool list is a written district list of the AI tools that staff and students may use, together with the rules for each one. It tells teachers which tools are safe to use with student information and gives the district a way to say no to tools that have not been checked. It matters because without it the choice falls to each teacher, which the text says is exactly what the FTC advises against.

crumbs.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule

sections.body: The approved tool list is a written record of which AI tools staff and students may use and what the rules are for each one. It does two jobs at once, because it tells teachers which tools are safe to use with student information and it gives the district a way to refuse tools nobody has checked. The problem it solves is that without such a list the decision falls to each individual teacher. The text states that this is exactly what the FTC advises against. A list also creates a repeatable path, so a tool is added after a short review rather than by default.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: A tool reaches the list only after a short, repeatable review. Someone checks the age rules, reads the privacy terms, confirms whether a signed data privacy agreement exists, and tests the tool with the kind of task teachers will use it for. The text points to Figure 3.3 for the steps, and it says the review does not need to take months, but it does need a named owner, usually the technology director, and a record of the decision. The list also needs a front door for requests, with a simple request form, a promised response time, and a clear answer of approved, approved with limits, or not approved. The text does not set this out by grade band, so the same process covers tools used by staff and by students, and the goal is to make the approved path the easiest path.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers no study, figure or finding for this idea beyond the review steps it points to in Figure 3.3, so it rests on practice rather than research. The only outside reference it makes is to the FTC, which the text says advises against leaving the choice of tools to each teacher. No numbers, dates or research results are given for the list itself.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main risk the text names is that without a list the choice falls to each teacher, which is the situation the FTC advises against. A second risk is that teachers will work around the list if there is no easy way to ask about a new tool, which is why the text calls for a request form, a promised response time and a clear answer. The decisions stay with people, since a named owner, usually the technology director, runs the review and keeps a record of it, and a person gives the answer of approved, approved with limits, or not approved. The text does not claim that a list removes the need for judgement, only that it makes the safe path the easiest one.
